title: Two-way Binding
summary: Keep a value and the screen in sync, in both directions at once.
heading: Two-way Binding

blocks.text: Property binding sends data into the view; event binding sends events out. Two-way binding does both at once: the class updates the view, and the view updates the class — they stay in sync automatically.

blocks.caption: The value and the view update each other.

blocks.text: The syntax is [( )] — square brackets (property in) plus parentheses (event out). People call it the "banana in a box".
Two-way binding is sugar. [(value)] expands to a property binding plus an event binding named valueChange — these two lines do exactly the same thing:
Rule: [(thing)] works when something has both a thing input and a thingChange output.

sections.title: Example 1: ngModel on a form input

blocks.text: The most common two-way binding is [(ngModel)] on an <input> — type in the box and the class value updates live. Needs FormsModule.
Run the live version in the next example — it uses [value] + (input), which is exactly what [(ngModel)] does under the hood.
To see the two halves clearly, here's the same input written as a property binding plus an event binding — no ngModel at all.

sections.title: Example 3: two-way on your own component

blocks.text: You can give your own component a two-way property with the model() function. It creates both the input and the matching ...Change output for you, so a parent can use [( )] on it.

blocks.label: counter.ts (child)

blocks.text: Click the child's button and the parent's total updates too — because model() binds both ways.

sections.title: Example 4: a toggle switch with model()

blocks.text: A reusable on/off switch. The child owns the button; the parent reads and sets the value through two-way binding.

sections.title: Example 5: a star rating with model()

blocks.text: model() shines for custom input controls. This star rating both shows the current value and reports changes — all through one two-way binding.
